descripcion_es: Greetings, goodbyes, personal details and jobs.
resumen: Phrases to say hello and goodbye, and to say who you are, where you are from and what you do. They are the first sentences of any conversation.

explicacion.texto: In English the greeting changes with the time of day and how well you know the person. “Hello” is always fine; “Hi” is informal. “How do you do?” is very formal and you answer with the same phrase, not by saying how you are.

filas: greeting from 12 to 6 p.m. (es: Buenas tardes)
greeting in the evening, when you arrive (es: Buenas tardes / noches)
goodbye at night or before bed (es: Buenas noches)
goodbye until later / soon (es: Hasta luego / hasta pronto)
question about how someone feels (es: ¿Cómo estás?)
said when you meet someone for the first time (es: Encantado de conocerte)
said when you meet someone, very formal (es: Encantado)
How do you do? – How do you do?
to say your name (es: Me llamo… / Soy…)
to ask someone's name (es: ¿Cómo te llamas?)
to ask where someone comes from (es: ¿De dónde eres?)
to ask someone's age (es: ¿Cuántos años tienes?)
to ask someone's job (es: ¿A qué te dedicas?)
to say your job (es: Trabajo de / como…)
to say where your home is (es: Vivo en…)
with / without a husband or wife (es: Estoy casado / soltero)
to introduce another person (es: Te presento a…)
to ask for the letters of a word (es: ¿Me lo deletreas?)

items: Jobs take an article: I'm a doctor, She's an architect.
Use be for age: I am 30, not “I have 30”.
Nationalities and languages have a capital letter: Spanish, English, French.
first name = your given name (es: nombre); surname / last name = your family name (es: apellido).

ejemplos.frase: Hi, I'm Carmen. Nice to meet you.
ejemplos.traduccion: Hola, soy Carmen. Encantada de conocerte.
Te presento a mi hermana, Laura.

ejemplos.frase: I'm from Valencia, but I live in London.
ejemplos.traduccion: Soy de Valencia, pero vivo en Londres.

ejemplos.frase: She's a nurse at the local hospital.
ejemplos.traduccion: Es enfermera en el hospital de la zona.

ejemplos.frase: How are you today? – Not bad, thanks. And you?
ejemplos.traduccion: ¿Qué tal estás hoy? – Nada mal, gracias. ¿Y tú?

errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Use be for age, not have.
Jobs in the singular take a/an.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Good night! (al llegar a una cena)
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Good night is only for saying goodbye.

ejercicios.explicacion: This is the basic phrase in the card to say your name: My name is… (or, more informal, I'm…). The clue is the possessive my, which needs a noun after it: my name. Name is your name in general; to be more exact, first name is your given name and surname or last name is your family name.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: My name is… is the phrase to say your name.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Calque of Spanish “me llamo”: My called is David does not exist. You say My name is… or I'm called…
Surname is your family name; David is a first name, so the word is name.

glosario.definicion_l: a language unit by which a person or thing is known · a person's reputation

ejercicios.explicacion: The card says that jobs in the singular take the indefinite article: She's an architect, I'm a doctor. The choice between a and an depends on the first sound of the next word, not the letter: architect starts with a vowel sound /ɑː/, so it takes an. Spanish says “es arquitecta” without an article, so Spanish speakers tend to leave it out.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Architect starts with a vowel sound, so it takes an.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Architect starts with a vowel sound: an architect.
The would mean a specific architect we already know; to say someone's job, use a/an.

glosario.definicion_l: someone who creates plans to be used in making something (such as buildings)

ejercicios.frase: Where are you ___? – I'm from Bilbao.
ejercicios.explicacion: Where are you from? is the fixed question in the card to ask where someone comes from. The preposition from (origin) stays at the end of the question, which is common in English. The answer confirms it: I'm from Bilbao. In Spanish the preposition goes at the beginning (“¿de dónde?”), and that is why learners leave it out or put it first.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Where are you from? asks about origin.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Of does not express origin; for origin, use from.
Where are you come is not grammatical; with are the preposition is from (or Where do you come from?).

ejercicios.frase: It's 9 a.m. You arrive at the office and say: «___, everyone!»
ejercicios.explicacion: The table in the card divides greetings by time: Good morning until twelve, Good afternoon from twelve to six and Good evening when you arrive in the evening. The clue is 9 a.m., which is in the morning, so the answer is Good morning. Everyone means “all the people” and you use it to speak to a group.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In the morning you say Good morning.
ejercicios.traduccion: Son las 9 de la mañana. Llegas a la oficina y dices: «¡Buenos días a todos!»

por_opcion.Good morning: Correct: it is the morning greeting, until midday.
por_opcion.Good night: It is not a greeting when you arrive: you use it to say goodbye at night or before going to bed.
por_opcion.Good evening: It is a greeting when you arrive, but late in the day or at night, not at nine in the morning.

glosario.definicion_l: a conventional expression of greeting or farewell, used to wish someone a good morning

ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that you answer Nice to meet you by repeating the same phrase with too: Nice to meet you too. Too, at the end, means “also”, like Spanish “igualmente”. Meet, here, means “to see someone for the first time”. The other options answer different questions.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Answer by repeating the phrase with too.

Correct: it repeats the phrase with too, as the card says.
It is an answer to How are you?, not to an introduction.
It is a way to say goodbye; it makes no sense just after someone is introduced to you.

glosario.definicion_l: to a degree exceeding normal or proper limits · in addition

ejercicios.frase: What do you ___? – I'm a lawyer.
ejercicios.explicacion: What do you do? is the fixed question in the card to ask about someone's job. The first do is the auxiliary for the question and the second is the verb “do”. Literally it is “what do you do?”, but it means “what is your job?”, and the answer I'm a lawyer confirms it. A lawyer works in law (es: abogado).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: What do you do? asks about someone's job.

por_opcion.do: Correct: What do you do? is the phrase to ask about someone's job.
por_opcion.make: Make means “to produce, to build something”; What do you make? would ask what you produce, not your job.
por_opcion.work: What do you work? is not grammatical; you say Where do you work? or What do you work as?.

glosario.definicion_l: a professional person authorized to practice law; conducts lawsuits or gives legal advice

ejercicios.frase: You leave a party at midnight and say: «___!»
ejercicios.explicacion: The card separates Good evening, used when you arrive, and Good night, used to say goodbye at night or before going to bed. The clue is leave (go away) and midnight: it is a goodbye at night, so the answer is Good night. In Spanish “buenas noches” works for both, and that is where the confusion comes from.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Good night is a goodbye at night.
ejercicios.traduccion: Te vas de una fiesta a medianoche y dices: «¡Buenas noches!»

por_opcion.Good night: Correct: it is the goodbye at night.
por_opcion.Good evening: It is a greeting when you arrive in the evening, not a goodbye.
por_opcion.Good afternoon: It is an afternoon greeting (from about twelve to six); it is not for midnight or for saying goodbye.

glosario.definicion_l: the period of time during which you are absent from work or duty · permission to do something
12 o'clock at night; the middle of the night

ejercicios.explicacion: The card warns that age uses the verb be, not have: I am 40. You can add years old at the end (I'm 40 years old), but never years alone. The calque of Spanish “tengo 40 años” is one of the most typical mistakes of Spanish speakers.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: age uses be, I'm 40.
Years needs old after it: I'm 40 years old, or simply I'm 40.
It still uses have: for age the verb is be.

ejercicios.explicacion: According to the card, jobs in the singular take a/an: My brother is a doctor. Doctor starts with a consonant sound, so it takes a. In Spanish the job has no article (“es médico”), so learners leave it out. Doctor is also used as a title.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Jobs in the singular take the article a/an.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: the article a is missing before the job.
Doctor starts with a consonant sound: a doctor.
The would mean a specific doctor; to say someone's job, use a.

glosario.definicion_l: (Roman Catholic Church) a title conferred on 33 saints who distinguished themselves through the orthodoxy of their theological teaching · a licensed medical practitioner

ejercicios.frase: Where do you come? – I come from Chile.
respuestas: Where do you come from? – I come from Chile.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card gives two ways to ask about origin: Where are you from? and Where do you come from?. With the verb come, the preposition from is necessary and goes at the end of the question. The answer already uses it correctly (I come from Chile), so you only need to add from to the question.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To ask about origin with come you need from at the end: Where do you come from?

errores_previstos.respuesta: Where do you come? – I come from Chile.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: from is missing at the end of the question.

errores_previstos.respuesta: From where do you come? – I come from Chile.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Calque of Spanish “¿de dónde…?”: in English from goes at the end, Where do you come from?

errores_previstos.respuesta: Where are you come from? – I come from Chile.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It mixes two phrases: either Where are you from? or Where do you come from?

ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that in questions the verb be goes before the subject and the preposition stays at the end. The order is Where + are + you + from. Spanish speakers tend to start with the preposition, as in “¿de dónde…?”, or to leave the subject before the verb.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In questions the verb be goes before the subject and the preposition at the end.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Calque of Spanish: from goes at the end of the question.
In a direct question are goes before you.

ejercicios.explicacion: To introduce another person, the card gives the phrase This is…, like Spanish “te presento a…” or “este es…”. After it comes the person: my friend Paul. In English you use this even when the person is in front of you, not he is, which sounds like a description, not an introduction.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: This is… is for introducing another person.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Is goes right after this: This is my friend Paul.
It would be a question (is this my friend Paul?), not an introduction.

glosario.definicion_l: a member of the Religious Society of Friends founded by George Fox (the Friends have never called themselves Quakers) · a person you know well and regard with affection and trust

ejercicios.explicacion: The card gives This is… as the phrase to introduce someone. The gap needs the verb be in the third person: is. Colleague means “a person you work with” (not a friend; in informal English a friend is a mate or buddy). To introduce someone you do not use he/she is, but this is.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To introduce someone, use This is…
ejercicios.traduccion: Esta es mi compañera de trabajo, Sarah.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is singular: This is.
This it's is not grammatical: this is already the subject and you only need the verb, is.

glosario.definicion_l: an associate that one works with · a person who is member of one's class or profession

ejercicios.explicacion: According to the card, How are you? asks how the person feels, not who they are or where they are from. The usual answer is short and friendly: Fine, thanks. And you?, returning the question. Fine means “well”; Very well or Not bad are also possible.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: How are you? asks how someone feels, not who they are.

por_opcion.Fine, thanks. And you?: Correct: it says how you are and returns the question, as people usually do.
It answers What do you do? (your job), not how you are.
It answers Where are you from? (your origin), not how you are.

glosario.definicion_l: being satisfactory or in satisfactory condition · minutely precise especially in differences in meaning

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the word that means “family name” (es: apellido).
ejercicios.frase: My first name is Elena and my ___ is Ruiz.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that first name is your given name and surname or last name is your family name; both forms are accepted. Surname is more British and last name more American. Be careful not to translate “apellido” as name, which is your name in general, or as second name, which usually means your second given name.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Surname or last name is your family name.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi nombre es Elena y mi apellido es Ruiz.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Second name usually means your second given name; the family name is surname or last name.
Name is your name in general; for the family name, use surname or last name.
You can say family name, but family alone only means the group of relatives.

glosario.definicion_l: the name that precedes the surname

descripcion_larga_es: Saying hello, saying goodbye and introducing yourself are the first sentences of any conversation and any oral exam. English uses different greetings for the time of day and the level of formality, and it has fixed phrases that you cannot translate word for word. Spanish speakers make calques: “I have 40 years”, “I am doctor” or confusing Good evening (greeting) with Good night (goodbye).

contexto.que_es: It is the set of phrases to say hello and goodbye, ask how someone is and give basic personal details: name, origin, age, job and where you live. It also includes how to introduce another person (This is…).
contexto.por_que_importa: It is the first impression in a meeting, an interview or at the start of an oral exam, and a mistake here is noticed at once. Calques like “I have 40 years”, or answering “How do you do?” by saying how you are, can sound funny or unprofessional. Choosing the right greeting for the time and the situation shows fluency from the first sentence.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: When you arrive somewhere, meet someone, start a phone call or an email and say goodbye. The signals are the time of day (morning, afternoon, evening), the level of formality (Hi versus Good morning, How do you do?) and the type of question (How are you? asks how you feel; What do you do? asks about your job). Spanish speakers tend to translate “buenas noches” always as Good night, but when you arrive you say Good evening.
